unit.title: Perform manual heating and thermal cutting

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan and lead manual heating and thermal cutting work. You will learn to choose between oxy-fuel and plasma, nest parts and do the sums for kerf, time and gas, handle oxygen, acetylene and LPG safely, check the outfit, cut to a drawing and judge the cut face, preheat and check temperatures, use heat to free and fit parts, flame straighten distorted steel, use a plasma cutter well, and supervise, record and report the work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **manual heating and thermal cutting** at the level of a leading hand: planning a cutting job and doing the sums, choosing between oxy-fuel and plasma, setting up and checking the equipment, cutting to a drawing and a quality standard, preheating, heating to free or fit parts, flame straightening, and supervising and reporting on the work.

At Level 2 you learned to light a torch, set a flame and make a clean cut. At Level 3 you must also explain **why** the process works, choose the best method for each job, plan the work so material and gas are not wasted, judge the quality of a cut against the drawing, and keep a team safe while they do it.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and fabricators and maintenance welders who cut, heat and straighten steel and lead others doing it.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawing, choose the process, nest the parts, allow for the kerf, plan the cut order, work out time, gas and cost.
Work safely and protect others
Run hot work controls and fire watch, control fumes from coatings and stainless steel, use the right PPE and filter shades.
Handle gases and check equipment
Know how oxygen, acetylene and LPG are held in their cylinders; judge contents; store cylinders; check hoses, nozzles, regulators and flashback arrestors.
Cut with oxy-fuel
Explain how the cut works and which metals it will not cut; choose the nozzle and pressures; cut straight, bevelled and shaped parts.
Judge cut quality
Read the cut face, name the faults and their causes, measure parts against the tolerance, and deal with hardened edges.
Heat and preheat
Preheat to a procedure and check the temperature; heat to free or fit parts; avoid overheating.
Flame straighten
Measure distortion, plan and make V, line and spot heats, and check the result.
Cut with plasma
Set up, use and look after a plasma cutter, and get a good cut on stainless steel, aluminium and thin plate.
Supervise and report
Brief and watch a team, stop unsafe work, keep inspection, heating and gas records, and report incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, gases and cylinders, equipment checks, preheat and manual heating, flame straightening, how cutting works, cut quality, plasma cutting, supervision and reporting, with some sums.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example HAZ, dross, drag lines, stand-off, martensite, tabs, LPG, SDS) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: a planned, nested oxy-fuel cutting job from 10 mm plate with an inspection sheet and gas record; and flame straightening a bowed welded tee and preheating a thick plate, with a heating record.

blocks.note: Many questions ask "why". Learn the reasons: why the oxide must melt below the metal, why a V heat stops short of the far edge, why a pulley is heated fast, why LPG cannot be judged by its gauge. If you know the reason, you can answer the question however it is worded.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the job and doing the sums

head: Job
Best choice
Why
rows: Carbon or mild steel, about 6 mm and thicker, especially thick plate
Oxy-fuel
Steel burns in the oxygen jet and its oxide runs out; cheap; cuts very thick plate; no power needed
Stainless steel
Plasma (or mechanical cutting)
Its chromium oxide melts far above the steel and will not run out of the cut, so oxy-fuel cannot cut it properly
Aluminium and copper alloys
Plasma (or a saw)
High-melting oxide on aluminium; both carry heat away too fast for oxy-fuel
Thin carbon steel sheet (up to about 6 mm)
Plasma, or mechanical cutting
Narrow kerf, fast, little heat and distortion
Cast iron
Plasma, saw, or abrasive disc
Its high carbon makes it melt before it can burn, so oxy-fuel will not cut it cleanly
Straight cuts in sheet, many parts
Guillotine (mechanical)
No heat, no slag, no HAZ

blocks.p: Plasma machines are sized by current and the thickness they can cut. A plasma set big enough for very thick carbon steel costs far more than an oxy-fuel outfit, so oxy-fuel stays the usual choice for thick plate.

ul: **Nesting**: lay the parts out close together on the plate, sharing edges where you can, to use the plate well and cut waste.

The **kerf** is the width of metal removed by the cut. Its width depends on the nozzle (the chart gives it) and is often about 1.5–4 mm for oxy-fuel. Cut on the **waste side** of every line, so each part keeps its full size.
Leave room for the kerf between parts: one kerf for every cut.

Plan the **cut order** so the plate stays stiff as long as possible: cut holes and inside shapes before the outside profile, work from the free edge inwards, and cut strips before the plate is weakened.
Leave small uncut **tabs** (bridges) to hold a part in the plate until the last cut, so it does not drop or move.
Long, narrow strips bow as they are cut. Cutting both edges at once with two torches, cutting from a wide plate with tabs, or cutting in short steps reduces this.

head: Sum
Method
Worked example
rows: Plate used for strips
Number of strips × (strip width + kerf)
5 strips 120 mm wide, kerf 2.5 mm: 5 × 122.5 = **612.5 mm**
Total length of cut
Add up every cut
A plate 300 × 200 mm cut on all four sides: 300 + 200 + 300 + 200 = **1 000 mm**
Cutting time
Length of cut ÷ travel speed
7.2 m (7 200 mm) at 450 mm/min = **16 minutes**
Gas used
Rate × time
A nozzle using about 45 L/min of oxygen for 16 minutes = **720 litres**
Cost per hour
Cost ÷ hours
J$10 500 of oxygen lasting 7 hours = **J$1 500 an hour**
Oxygen left in a cylinder
Full contents × (gauge reading ÷ full pressure)
A cylinder holding 8 400 L at 200 bar reads 60 bar: 8 400 × 60 ÷ 200 = **2 520 L**
Tolerance check
Drawing size ± tolerance gives the limits
250 mm ± 1.5 mm: anything from 248.5 to 251.5 mm passes

blocks.note: Write the units at every step and change metres to millimetres (or the other way) before you divide. Most wrong answers in cutting sums come from mixing m and mm, or minutes and hours.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Read the drawing: material, thickness, part sizes, number off, tolerance
Choose the process and the nozzle and pressures from the maker's chart
Draw the nested layout, allowing for the kerf, and plan the cut order and tabs
Work out the length of cut, time and gas, and check there is enough gas in the cylinders
Write a short risk assessment and get any hot work permit
Share out the tasks: marking out, cutting, fire watch, cleaning, checking sizes
Brief the team and prepare the inspection sheet

blocks.p: Cutting and heating throw molten metal and sparks, make fumes from the metal and its coatings, and use gases that burn or feed a fire. The person leading the job plans the controls, briefs the team and checks them before the first light-up.

ul: Get a **hot work permit** where the site uses one. It names the area, the time, the fire precautions and the fire watch.
Clear or cover anything that can burn for at least **10 metres**, and further when cutting at height: sparks fall and scatter much further from a high level.
Cover or plug floor drains, gaps, cracks and openings. Sparks fall through them and can light gas, oil or rubbish below.
Cut over a cutting table with slats, or over sand or a steel tray, not straight onto a concrete floor: wet concrete can spall (burst) under the heat.
Keep extinguishers at hand and keep a **fire watch** during the work and for the time the permit sets after it, often 30–60 minutes, checking the area, below it and behind walls.

blocks.p: Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn far more fiercely. Clothing, hair and grease that would only smoulder in air flare up in oxygen-rich air.

ul: Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothing or a bench, to "freshen" the air in a tank or room, or to power air tools.
Never let oil or grease touch oxygen fittings, regulators or hoses.
Take hoses and torches out of a confined space at every break: a slow leak can fill it with oxygen or fuel gas.

head: Material
Hazard
Control
rows: Old paint (may contain lead)
Lead fume: poisoning over time
Test or strip the paint back from the cut line first; extraction; RPE as the risk assessment says
Galvanised (zinc-coated) steel
Zinc fume: metal fume fever
Remove the coating near the cut where you can; extraction; RPE
Stainless steel (plasma cutting)
Fume containing chromium compounds, some of which cause cancer
Extraction at the cut, a water table or downdraught table; respirator if needed
Oily, greasy or plastic-coated steel
Smoke and toxic gases
Clean or strip it first
Any unknown coating or chemical
Unknown
Find out what it is from the owner and its **safety data sheet (SDS)** before cutting

head: Work
Typical eye protection
rows: Oxy-fuel cutting and heating
Gas goggles or a face shield of about shade 3–5 (darker for heavier work)
Plasma cutting
Shade chosen by the current: often about shade 5 up to about 40 A, 6 at about 40–60 A, 8 at about 60–300 A, and darker above that
Grinding and chipping
Clear safety glasses with a face shield over them

ul: Leather gloves, flame-resistant clothing with no turn-ups or open pockets, leather boots, and a cap.
Ear protection for plasma cutting and grinding: both are loud.
Take lighters out of your pockets before you cut.

blocks.note: Shades 3–5 are for gas work only. They do **not** protect your eyes from a plasma arc at higher currents or from an electric welding arc. Follow the shade chart for the process and the current.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Put up screens and barriers, and keep the public, customers, guests and other trades away from sparks and falling cut-offs.
Plan where cut pieces will fall, and keep that drop zone clear and barriered.
Warn people nearby before you start, and keep walkways free of hoses.

sections.title: Gases, cylinders and the cutting outfit

head: Gas
How it is held
How to judge what is left
Points to know
rows: Oxygen
Compressed gas at high pressure (often about 150–200 bar when full)
The contents gauge: pressure falls in step with the gas left, so half the full pressure means about half full
Keep oil and grease away; never use it as compressed air
Acetylene
Dissolved in acetone, held in a porous filling inside the cylinder
By weight (the gauge also changes with temperature)
Store and use **upright**; working pressure kept low (never above about 1 bar); do not draw it off too fast, or acetone comes out with the gas
LPG (propane)
Liquefied petroleum gas, held as a **liquid** under its own pressure
Only by **weighing**: weigh the cylinder and take away the tare (empty) weight stamped on it
The gauge reads about the same until the liquid is nearly gone; heavier than air, so leaks collect in drains, pits and low places

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: LPG left = scale reading − tare weight
A cylinder weighs 50 kg and its tare is 32 kg: 50 − 32 = **18 kg** of gas left
Acetylene draw-off limit (common rule: about one-seventh of the contents per hour; follow the supplier's figure)
A cylinder holds about 7 000 L, so it should give no more than about 1 000 L an hour. A heating nozzle using 1 800 L an hour needs **2 cylinders** on a manifold

head: Point
Acetylene
Propane (LPG)
rows: Flame temperature
Hottest (about 3 100 °C)
Lower (about 2 800 °C)
Preheat and piercing
Fast; good for short cuts, piercing and bevels
Slower to start each cut
Oxygen needed
Less
Much more oxygen for the preheat flame
Cost
Higher
Lower; suits long cuts in thick plate and heating
Equipment
Acetylene regulator and nozzles
A **regulator and nozzles made for propane**; check the hoses and arrestors are rated for it
Leaks
Slightly lighter than air
Heavier than air: collects low down

ul: Store **upright and secured** (chained or in a rack), with valve caps or guards on cylinders not in use.
Keep oxygen apart from fuel gases (often at least about 6 metres, or behind a fire-resistant wall).
In a dry, ventilated place, out of the sun, away from heat, drains and pits.
Keep full and empty cylinders apart, and label empties.

head: Part
Check
If faulty
rows: Regulators
Right gas, gauges readable, no damage; threads clean
Take out of use and return for repair
Flashback arrestors (at the regulators) and non-return valves (at the torch)
Fitted on both gases; in date; tested or replaced at the intervals the maker gives, because they can clog or wear and then fail without warning
Replace
Hoses
No cuts, burns, cracks, bulges or worn cover; correct crimped fittings
Take out of use and fit a new hose assembly; never tape a damaged hose
Torch and valves
Valves turn freely and shut off fully; no leaks
Repair or replace
Cutting nozzle
Right size for the plate; holes clean and round; the **seat** (where it meets the torch) undamaged
A damaged seat can leak gas and start a fire: replace it

blocks.p: After fitting the parts, open the cylinder valves slowly, set the pressures, and **leak test** every joint with leak-detection fluid. Never test with a flame.

head: Flame
How it looks
Use
rows: Neutral
Clear, rounded inner cones; no feather
Preheat flames for cutting; most heating
Carburising (excess fuel)
A white feather round the inner cone
Not used for cutting steel
Oxidising (excess oxygen)
Short, sharp, pointed inner cone; harsh hiss
Not for general cutting; it can make the cut edges rough

head: Event
What happens
What to do
rows: Backfire
A loud pop; the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle for a moment
Shut the torch valves, find the cause (nozzle too close to the work, overheated, blocked or loose nozzle, wrong pressures), put it right, then relight
Flashback
The flame burns back into the torch or hoses, often with a squeal or hiss, and the handle gets hot

Close the torch valves at once (oxygen first, unless the maker says otherwise), then the cylinder valves; move back; tag the set out of use; have the torch, hoses and arrestors checked or replaced before reuse

blocks.note: Repeated backfires on one torch are a warning. Stop and find the cause, and record it: the torch, the nozzle, what happened and what you did. A torch that keeps backfiring may be heading for a flashback.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: How oxy-fuel cutting works, and cutting technique

blocks.p: An oxy-fuel torch does not melt its way through steel. The **preheat flames** heat a spot to its ignition temperature (a bright red heat, roughly 870–900 °C). Then a jet of pure **cutting oxygen** makes the hot iron burn. The burning gives off heat, which keeps the reaction going, and the jet blows the molten oxide (slag) out of the bottom of the cut.
This works on carbon and low-alloy steel because:

ul: the steel burns in oxygen at a temperature **below** its melting point, so it burns before it melts;
its oxide melts at a **lower** temperature than the steel, so the oxide is fluid and is blown out;
burning gives off enough heat to keep the cut going;
steel does not carry heat away too fast.

head: Metal
Why oxy-fuel will not cut it cleanly
rows: Stainless steel
Chromium forms an oxide that melts far above the steel; it stays solid and blocks the cut
Aluminium
Its oxide melts at about 2 050 °C, three times the metal's melting point; the metal just melts and runs
Cast iron
Its high carbon makes it melt before it reaches its burning temperature, and its graphite gets in the way
Copper and brass
They carry heat away too fast and do not burn freely in oxygen

ul: Use the **maker's chart**: it gives the nozzle size, the oxygen and fuel pressures and a typical speed for each plate thickness.
Thicker plate needs a **larger nozzle** (a bigger cutting oxygen hole) and a **slower** travel speed.
Set **neutral** preheat flames. Keep the tips of the inner cones about 2–3 mm above the plate.
Rusty or heavily scaled plate needs a little more preheat, or cleaning first.

head: Point
Good practice
rows: Starting at an edge
Heat the edge to bright red, open the cutting oxygen fully with the lever, and start moving as the cut goes through
Piercing a hole
Heat the spot, raise the nozzle a little and tilt it slightly as you open the oxygen so the slag blows away from the nozzle, then lower it and go on; start holes in the waste
Long straight cuts
Run the torch against a straight-edge guide or use a roller (wheel) attachment: it keeps the nozzle height and angle steady
Circles and shapes
Use a circle-cutting attachment or a template
Bevels
Tilt the nozzle to the bevel angle and keep it there; a guide or a cutting trolley helps
Steadiness
Brace your arm, stand comfortably, and move smoothly; check you can reach the whole cut before you start

blocks.note: Listen and look. A good cut gives a steady roar, and the sparks leave the bottom of the plate at a slight angle back, against the direction of travel. Sparks blowing back up out of the top mean the cut has not gone through: slow down.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: The effects of heat on the steel

blocks.p: The cut edge is heated and then cooled fast by the cold plate around it. The band of metal beside the cut that has been changed by the heat, but not melted, is the **heat-affected zone (HAZ)**.

ul: On **mild steel** the HAZ is narrow and does little harm.
On **high-carbon, alloy and thick steels**, fast cooling forms **martensite**, a very hard, brittle structure. The edge can crack, sometimes hours later, or when it is bent, drilled or welded.
**Preheating** before cutting slows the cooling and stops this. The procedure gives the temperature.
If a hardened or cracked edge has already been cut, grind the hard layer off before welding or bending, and preheat next time.

blocks.p: A good cut saves grinding and fits up first time. Judge each cut face against the quality standard the job uses, or against a sample of a good cut kept at the cutting table.

ul: Top edge sharp and square, not melted or rounded.
Face square to the plate (or at the bevel angle), smooth and flat.
**Drag lines** (the curved lines left by the oxygen stream) fine and nearly straight up and down.
Bottom edge clean, with little or no **dross** (slag and re-solidified metal) stuck to it, and any that is there coming off easily.
No gouges, notches or cracks.

head: What you see
Likely causes
Correction
rows: Top edge melted and rounded, sometimes with beads of metal
Preheat flames too strong; nozzle too close; travel too slow
Right nozzle and pressures; inner cones 2–3 mm off; travel faster
Heavy dross stuck hard to the bottom edge
Travel too slow or too fast; cutting oxygen too low; dirty nozzle
Check the oxygen pressure; clean or change the nozzle; find the right speed
Drag lines curved strongly backwards; bottom corner left uncut at the end
Travel too fast
Slow down; pause at the end of the cut until it breaks through
Face hollowed out (concave) from top to bottom
Cutting oxygen pressure too high; nozzle too big for the plate
Lower the oxygen to the chart figure or fit the right nozzle
Face bevelled the same way along the whole cut
Torch not held square to the plate
Use a guide; check the nozzle is square with a small square
Gouges or notches at intervals along the face
Unsteady or jerky travel; flame popping; slag or spatter in the nozzle
Brace your arm, use a guide; clean the nozzle; check pressures
Wide, uneven kerf
Damaged or dirty nozzle; nozzle too big; torch wandering
Clean or replace the nozzle; use the chart size; use a guide
Cracks or a very hard edge
High-carbon or alloy steel cut without preheat
Grind off the hard layer; preheat next time

blocks.note: Change **one thing at a time**, make a short test cut, and compare it with the good sample. If you change the speed and the pressure together, you will not know which one fixed it.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Let the parts cool; chip and grind off the slag and dross
Measure each part against the drawing with a rule or tape and a square
Check the cut faces against the standard or the sample: top edge, squareness, drag lines, dross, gouges, cracks
Record the results for each part on an inspection sheet, with the job number, date and your name
Parts too big or rough: grind or re-cut to size
Parts too small, cracked or badly gouged: reject tag, quarantine, report to the supervisor
Look for a pattern in the faults and put the cause right

head: Drawing says
Passes
Fails
rows: From 248.5 to 251.5 mm (for example 249.0 or 251.4 mm)
Below 248.5 or above 251.5 mm (for example 248.2 or 251.7 mm)
150 mm ± 1 mm
From 149 to 151 mm

blocks.note: A part that is too big can often be trimmed. A part that is too small usually cannot be saved. That is why you cut on the waste side of the line, and why the kerf is allowed for in the layout.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Manual heating, preheating and flame straightening

blocks.p: **Preheating** means warming the steel before it is cut or welded. Thick steel, high-carbon steel and many alloy and high-strength steels harden if they cool fast, because the cold metal around the hot area draws the heat away. A hard edge or weld can crack. Preheat slows the cooling and, for welding, also lets hydrogen escape and cuts distortion.

ul: The **procedure** (WPS, cutting procedure or drawing) gives the preheat temperature. Never guess it.
Heat evenly, with a heating nozzle or a large flame kept moving, over a band on each side of the cut line or joint, and **through the thickness**, not just the surface.
Measure the temperature **a set distance back from the joint** (often about 75 mm, or as the procedure says), and on the far face where you can, after the heat has had time to spread.
Keep it at temperature while the work is done; check again between passes.
Do not go above any maximum the procedure gives: overheating harms some steels.

head: Method
How it works
Points to know
rows: Temperature-indicating crayons
Stroke the crayon on the steel; it melts and leaves a wet, glossy mark when the steel is at or above its rated temperature, and a dry chalky mark below it
Use two crayons to bracket a range (one at the minimum, one at the maximum). Do not mark inside the weld groove.
Contact thermometer (surface probe or thermocouple)
A probe pressed on the steel gives a reading
Accurate if it is in calibration and held on long enough
Infrared (non-contact) thermometer
Reads the heat given off by the surface
Shiny or bright surfaces can read far too low; set it for steel and check it against a contact reading
Colour of the steel
Glow colours
Only for high temperatures (dull red and above), and hard to judge in bright daylight. Never use it for preheat.

blocks.note: Spitting on the steel, holding a hand near it, or judging by colour are not ways to prove a preheat. A supervisor needs a reading that can be written down and checked.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Heating to free or fit parts

blocks.p: Steel grows when it is heated, by about **0.012 mm per metre for every 1 °C** (about 12 millionths of its size per °C). You can use this to free seized parts and to fit tight ones.

head: Job
Method
Why
rows: A pulley, gear or coupling seized on a shaft
Heat the outer part **quickly** and evenly, all round, then draw it off with a puller
The outer part grows and its bore opens before the heat soaks into the shaft and makes it grow too
A seized nut
Heat the nut quickly, not the bolt
The nut grows away from the bolt threads
Fitting a tight (shrink-fit) collar or hub
Heat the hub evenly to the temperature worked out, slide it on, let it cool
As it cools it shrinks and grips the shaft

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: Growth = size × 0.000012 × temperature rise
A hub bore of 100 mm heated by 100 °C grows 100 × 0.000012 × 100 = **0.12 mm**
Temperature rise needed = growth needed ÷ (size × 0.000012)
To open a 120 mm bore by 0.18 mm: 0.18 ÷ (120 × 0.000012) = **125 °C** rise, plus a little more for clearance while fitting

ul: Holding steel very hot for a long time makes its grains grow coarse, which weakens it and makes it less tough.
Uneven heating distorts parts.
Steel heated until it sparks and its surface bubbles is **burnt**: it is spoiled and must be scrapped.
Quenched and tempered high-strength steels lose strength if heated above the limit their maker gives.
Never heat near a tyre, a sealed container, a hydraulic cylinder or anything holding gas or liquid under pressure: it can burst.

blocks.p: Flame straightening uses heat and shrinkage to pull distorted steel back into line. A small area is heated quickly. The cold metal around it stops it growing outwards, so the hot metal is squeezed and gets slightly thicker (upset). When it cools, it shrinks, and pulls the part **towards the heated side**. So you heat the **long (convex) side** of a bend.

flow: Support the part so it can move, and keep people clear of where it will move
Check the steel type: high-strength steels need a written procedure and a lower temperature limit
Mark points along the part (for example every 100 mm) and measure the bow at each with a straight edge or a string line and spacer blocks
Mark the convex side and record the readings

head: Pattern
Used for
How
rows: V (wedge) heat
Bars, flat bar edgeways, the webs of beams and tees bowed in their own plane

Wide end of the V at the convex edge; the point about **two-thirds to three-quarters** of the way across. Heat from the point out to the wide end. The cool metal past the point acts as a **hinge**, so the bar bends back instead of just shrinking.
Strip (line) heat
Flanges, and with V heats on beams; angular distortion of a plate beside a weld
A narrow band heated along or across the convex side
Spot heats
Bulges (buckles) in thin plate and panels

Small spots on the bulge, one at a time, each allowed to cool before the next. Small spots are held tight by the cold metal round them, so they shrink and pull the slack out; one big heat would just let the panel grow and buckle more.

ul: Mild steel: usually no hotter than a **dull red** (about 600–650 °C), checked with temperature crayons. High-strength steels: the lower limit their procedure gives.
Heat quickly, so the heat stays where you want it; a slow heat spreads and does less.
Let each heat **cool in air** before you measure again. Never spray water on red-hot high-strength steel: quick cooling can make it hard and brittle.
Do not keep reheating the same spot. If more correction is needed, place the next heat at a new point along the bow.
Make fewer, well-placed heats rather than many: every heat leaves some change in the steel.

blocks.note: Straightening by heat is slow on purpose. Heat, cool, measure, record, and only then decide on the next heat. Rushing leads to over-correction, which then needs heats on the other side.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A heating record gives the part, the steel, the readings before, the heat pattern and positions, the temperatures checked, the readings after each heat, and the final result against the tolerance.

A plasma cutter passes an electric arc through a gas (usually compressed air on workshop machines) forced through a small hole in a copper **nozzle**. The arc heats the gas until it becomes **plasma**: very hot, electrically conducting, ionised gas. The narrow jet **melts** the metal and blows it out of the cut. It does not depend on the metal burning, so it cuts stainless steel, aluminium, copper and any metal that conducts electricity.

ul: A **pilot arc** inside the torch starts the plasma; when the torch is near the work, the arc transfers to the work clamp circuit and cuts.
Plasma suits thin and medium plate and non-ferrous metals: narrow kerf, fast, little heat and distortion.

head: Part
Job
Signs of wear
rows: Electrode
Carries the arc; has a small insert that wears into a pit
Pit worn deeper than the maker allows; hard starting
Swirl ring
Spins the gas round the electrode
Cracks, blocked holes
Nozzle (tip)
Shapes the arc through its small hole
Hole worn oval or enlarged; the arc wanders; kerf wider and rougher; more bevel
Shield or retaining cap
Protects the nozzle and holds the parts
Spatter build-up, damage

blocks.note: Change consumables only with the power **switched off and isolated**. A plasma cutter's open-circuit voltage is much higher than a welding machine's (often a few hundred volts), so a shock from it is far more dangerous. Keep gloves dry and never touch the front of the torch with the power on.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Air must be **clean and dry**: water and oil in the air wear the electrode and nozzle fast and spoil the cut. Drain the filter and the compressor tank; fit a dryer where the air is wet.
Set the air pressure the maker gives, measured with air flowing. If the shop compressor also feeds other tools, pressure can drop during the cut.
Set the current for the metal and thickness from the maker's chart, and use the matching nozzle.
Fix the work clamp to clean metal on the job, near the cut.

Keep the **stand-off** (the distance from the torch to the plate) steady, as the maker gives; a guide or a stand-off roller helps. Drag the shield on the plate only where the maker allows it, usually at low current.
Hold the torch square to the plate. On most machines one side of the kerf comes out squarer than the other: keep the good side on the part.
Travel at a speed where the sparks leave the bottom at a slight angle back.

head: What you see
Likely cause
rows: Heavy, bubbly dross on the bottom that knocks off easily
Travel too slow
Small, hard bead of dross rolled on the bottom; sparks spraying up; cut not through
Travel too fast
Arc wandering; kerf wider and rougher than before; more bevel
Worn nozzle or electrode; stand-off too high
Spitting, sputtering arc; short consumable life
Wet or oily air; wrong pressure
Arc will not transfer
Work clamp loose or on dirty metal; stand-off too high

blocks.p: Some plasma tables have water under the plate to catch fume and dross. When **aluminium** is cut over water, the hot aluminium reacts with the water and gives off **hydrogen**, which can collect under the plate and explode. Follow the table maker's rules: keep the water moving or aerated, do not let aluminium dross build up, and clean the table out often.

ul: Filter shade to suit the current (see the safety section), not gas goggles.
Ear protection: plasma cutting is loud.
Fume extraction at the cut, especially for stainless steel, galvanised and painted steel.
Brief the job: the drawing, the plan, the hazards and controls, and each person's task (marking out, cutting, fire watch, cleaning, checking).
Check the set and the area yourself before the first light-up.

Watch the work. **Stop unsafe work at once**, put it right, explain why, and then let it go on. Cylinders lying on the floor, hoses across walkways, no fire watch, or a damaged hose in use are all stopped on the spot.
Coach one point at a time, and check each person's cuts against the sample.

blocks.note: Acetylene cylinders must be used upright: lying down, acetone can come out with the gas and damage the equipment or feed a fire. All cylinders must be secured so they cannot fall. If the trolley is in use, the job waits until the cylinders are properly secured.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Close the torch valves
Close both cylinder valves
Open the torch valves one at a time to bleed the hoses, then close them
Wind out the regulator adjusting screws
Coil the hoses and hang them up; store the torch
Mark hot parts HOT; leave them to cool in a safe place
Clean up slag and offcuts, and check the area for smouldering; keep fire watch for the permit's time
Plasma: switch off, isolate, drain the air filter, and report worn parts

head: Record
What goes on it
rows: Inspection sheet
Job, part numbers, measured sizes against tolerance, cut quality, pass or fail, rejects and their cause, date, name
Gas record
Cylinder contents before and after (gauge or weight), gas used, hours of cutting
Heating record
Part, steel, readings before and after, heat pattern, temperatures checked, result
Incident or near-miss report
Date, time, place, people, the equipment and its serial number, what happened, immediate action, likely cause, repairs, and what will stop it happening again; signed

blocks.p: Backfires, flashbacks, hose damage, small fires and any injury are all reported. A near miss reported today is an accident prevented tomorrow.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can choose between oxy-fuel, plasma and mechanical cutting for a job, and give the reason.
I can nest parts, allow for the kerf, plan the cut order and use tabs.
I can work out plate used, length of cut, cutting time, gas used, gas left and cost per hour.
I can plan hot work safely, including drains, work at height and the fire watch.
I can explain the dangers of oxygen enrichment and of fumes from coatings and stainless steel.
I can explain how oxygen, acetylene and LPG are held, and judge the contents of each.
I can store cylinders and check regulators, arrestors, hoses and nozzles.
I can name the three flames and tell a backfire from a flashback, and act on each.
I can explain why oxy-fuel cuts steel but not stainless steel, aluminium or cast iron.
I can choose the nozzle, pressures and speed for a plate thickness.
I can read a cut face, name the faults and correct their causes.
I can explain the HAZ and martensite, and why some steels are preheated before cutting.
I can preheat to a procedure and check the temperature with crayons or a thermometer.
I can work out how much a part grows when heated, and use heat to free or fit parts.
I can measure distortion and plan V, strip and spot heats to straighten it.
I can set up, use and care for a plasma cutter and correct its faults.
I can supervise a cutting team, shut down safely and keep the records.

terms: Backfire
A pop in which the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle for a moment
Cutting oxygen
The jet of pure oxygen, released by the lever, that burns the steel and blows out the slag
Drag lines
The curved lines on a cut face left by the cutting oxygen stream
Dross
Slag and re-solidified metal stuck to the bottom edge of a cut
Flashback
The flame burning back into the torch or hoses
Flashback arrestor
A device at the regulator that stops a flashback reaching the cylinder
HAZ
Heat-affected zone: metal beside a cut or weld changed by heat but not melted
Kerf
The width of metal removed by a cut
LPG
Liquefied petroleum gas, such as propane, held as a liquid in the cylinder
Martensite
A very hard, brittle structure formed when hot high-carbon or alloy steel cools too fast
Nesting
Laying parts out close together on a plate to save material
Neutral flame
A flame with balanced oxygen and fuel; clear, rounded inner cones
Oxidising flame
A flame with more oxygen than fuel; short, sharp inner cone and a harsh hiss
Plasma
Very hot, ionised gas that conducts electricity
Preheat
Warming steel before cutting or welding to slow its cooling
SDS
Safety data sheet: the hazards of a substance and how to handle it
Spot heat
A small heat used to shrink a bulge out of thin plate
Stand-off
The distance from the end of a plasma torch to the plate
Tabs
Small uncut parts left to hold a part in the plate until the last cut
Tare weight
The weight of an empty cylinder, stamped on it
Temperature crayon
A crayon that melts at a rated temperature, used to check heat
V heat
A wedge-shaped heat used to straighten a bar or web bowed in its own plane

c1.title: Base plates and strips for a church hall in Albert Town
c1.text: Jermaine leads a team cutting parts from 12 mm mild steel plate for a church hall extension in Albert Town, Trelawny, using oxy-acetylene and a straight-edge guide. Four strips 150 mm wide are to come off one long edge, and the nozzle chart gives a kerf of about 2.5 mm. The job has about 8.1 m of cutting at about 450 mm per minute, and the nozzle uses about 45 litres of oxygen a minute. The oxygen cylinder holds about 9 000 litres at 200 bar when full and now reads 40 bar. Each base plate has four bolt holes, and the drawing gives 200 mm ± 1.5 mm for its sides.

c2.title: Fitting a coupling at a pumping station in Moneague
c2.text: Shanice must shrink-fit a steel coupling hub onto a pump shaft at a pumping station near Moneague, St Ann. The hub's bore is 100 mm, and it must grow by 0.15 mm to slide on with a little clearance. Steel grows by about 0.000012 of its size for each 1 °C. She will use a heating nozzle that burns about 1 600 litres of acetylene an hour, and each acetylene cylinder holds about 7 000 litres. She has temperature crayons rated 150 °C and 200 °C.

c3.title: Trainee cuts at a centre in Buff Bay
c3.text: At a training centre in Buff Bay, Portland, an instructor reviews three trainees' oxy-acetylene cuts in 20 mm mild steel plate. Tyrone's cut faces have drag lines that curve strongly backwards, and the bottom corner is left uncut at the end of each cut. Kayla cut freehand, and her faces have deep gouges at irregular intervals. Shanelle used the nozzle the chart lists for 6–10 mm plate; her cuts were slow, kept losing the cut, and left heavy dross.

c4.title: Straightening on a fishing boat at Whitehouse
c4.text: Kemoy is straightening a steel fishing boat at Whitehouse, Westmoreland. Welding new stiffeners has left a bulge in a panel of the 4 mm deck plate. A 75 mm × 8 mm flat bar rail has also bowed edgeways by about 9 mm over 1.5 m. Both are mild steel. After his first V heat on the rail has cooled, he measures the bow again and finds it is now about 5 mm.

c5.title: Plasma cutting at a sign shop in Green Island
c5.text: Dahlia plasma cuts letters from 3 mm aluminium and 2 mm stainless steel sheet on a water table at a sign shop in Green Island, Hanover. The shop compressor also runs a spray gun. Water is standing in the plasma cutter's air-filter bowl, the arc spits, and nozzles are wearing out within a day. A helper has been changing nozzles with the machine switched on so as not to lose time, and the bottom edges of the aluminium letters carry heavy, bubbly dross that knocks off easily.

questions.q: How much of the plate's width will the four strips use, allowing one kerf for each cut?
o: 600 mm
610 mm
620 mm
questions.why: Each strip needs its own width plus one kerf: 4 × (150 + 2.5) = 610 mm. Leaving out the kerf gives 600 mm and parts that come out short.

questions.q: Is there enough oxygen in the cylinder for the job?
o: No: 40 bar is too low a pressure to cut 12 mm plate at all
Yes: about 1 800 L are left, and about 810 L are needed
No: about 360 L are left, and about 810 L are needed
Yes: the cylinder still holds about 9 000 L of oxygen
questions.why: Oxygen is a compressed gas, so contents follow pressure: 9 000 × 40 ÷ 200 = 1 800 L. The cut takes 8 100 ÷ 450 = 18 minutes at 45 L/min, about 810 L. Keep a spare cylinder ready all the same.

questions.q: Each square has four bolt holes. Which should come first, the holes or the outline?
o: The outline, so the holes can be pierced on the bench
Either one, as long as a guide is used for each cut
The holes, while the part is still held by the plate
The outline, and then the holes are drilled to save gas
questions.why: Holes and inside shapes are cut first, while the part is held firm by the plate around it. Once the outline is cut, the part can move or drop, and piercing a loose part is harder and less accurate.

questions.q: One base plate measures 201.8 mm on a side. What should be done?
o: Pass it, as it is less than 2 mm over the drawing size
Scrap it at once and cut a new plate from the offcut
Grind it back within 198.5–201.5 mm, then check again
Pass it, and write the real size on the drawing
questions.why: The limits are 198.5 to 201.5 mm, so 201.8 mm is 0.3 mm too big. A part that is too big can be trimmed to size and re-measured; only a part that is too small usually has to be scrapped.

questions.q: About how much must the hub's temperature rise for the bore to grow 0.15 mm?
o: About 12.5 °C
About 63 °C
About 125 °C
About 1 250 °C
questions.why: Rise = growth ÷ (size × 0.000012) = 0.15 ÷ (100 × 0.000012) = 0.15 ÷ 0.0012 = 125 °C above the starting temperature. Check the sum by working it forwards: 100 × 0.000012 × 125 = 0.15 mm.

questions.q: What does the heating nozzle's gas use mean for the acetylene supply?
o: One cylinder is plenty, since it holds about 7 000 litres
Open the cylinder valve fully so that it gives more gas
Lay the cylinder down so that more gas can be drawn off
Join two cylinders on a manifold to share the draw-off
questions.why: A common rule is to draw no more than about one-seventh of the contents an hour, about 1 000 L from a 7 000 L cylinder. Drawing 1 600 L an hour from one cylinder pulls acetone out with the gas, so two cylinders are manifolded.

questions.q: Stroked on the hub, the 150 °C crayon leaves a wet, glossy mark and the 200 °C crayon a dry, chalky one. What does this show?
o: The hub is between 150 °C and 200 °C
The hub is still below 150 °C all through
The hub is already hotter than 200 °C
The two crayons have been mixed up
questions.why: A crayon melts when the steel is at or above its rating and leaves a dry mark below it. Using two crayons brackets the temperature: here it is at least 150 °C but not yet 200 °C.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the faults in Tyrone's cuts?
o: His preheat flames were set much too large
He travelled too fast for the plate
His cutting oxygen pressure was too high
His nozzle was held too close to the plate
questions.why: Drag lines that lag far behind, with the bottom corner left uncut, show the oxygen jet could not keep up with the torch. Slowing down, and pausing at the end until the cut breaks through, puts it right.

questions.q: What will most improve Kayla's cut faces?
o: Use a guide and brace her arm as she travels
Turn up the cutting oxygen so that it blows harder
Use a bigger nozzle so the cut is wider and easier
Travel faster so the torch has less time to wander
questions.why: Gouges at irregular intervals come from unsteady, jerky travel. A guide or roller holds the nozzle height and angle, and a braced arm and comfortable stance keep the movement smooth.

questions.q: What should Shanelle change first?
o: Raise the fuel gas pressure so the preheat flames are hotter
Hold the nozzle much closer so the inner cones touch the plate
Fit the nozzle the chart gives for 20 mm, with its pressures
Cut each line twice, going over it again from the other end
questions.why: A nozzle sized for thinner plate has too small a cutting oxygen hole to burn through 20 mm. The chart gives the nozzle size and pressures for each thickness: fit the right one first, then set the speed.

questions.q: Why should Kemoy use small spot heats on the deck bulge, not one large heat?
o: Cold steel round a small spot holds it, so it shrinks the bulge out
Small spots use far less gas, so the job will cost much less to do
A large heat would melt straight through the 4 mm plate very quickly
Small spots can be cooled with water, but large heats cannot be
questions.why: The cold metal round a small, quick heat stops it growing outwards, so it thickens slightly and then shrinks as it cools, drawing the slack out of the bulge. A big heat lets the whole panel expand and buckle further.

questions.q: After the first heat, the rail is still bowed about 5 mm. What should Kemoy do next?
o: Reheat the same V to a bright orange so that it pulls harder
Heat the concave edge of the rail to balance out the first heat
Hammer the rail cold where it is bowed until it is straight
Make a second V heat at a new point, then cool and measure
questions.why: Each heat corrects part of the bow. The next V goes at a new point along the bow, at no more than a dull red, and is left to cool in air before measuring. Heating the concave side would bend it the wrong way.

questions.q: Why does each V heat on the rail stop about two-thirds of the way across?
o: The far edge is too thin to take the heat without melting
It saves gas, as the far edge does not need any heat
So that the heat cannot travel along the rail to the welds
The cool far edge acts as a hinge so the rail bends back
questions.why: If the whole width were heated, it would simply shrink in length. Leaving cool metal past the point of the V gives a hinge, so the shrinking wide end pulls the rail round towards the heated edge.

questions.q: What should be done about cutting aluminium over the water table?
o: Cut it faster so that much less hot metal falls into the water
Keep the water moving and clean aluminium dross out often
Add a little oil to the water to stop any sparks
Raise the plate higher above the water with extra slats
questions.why: Hot aluminium reacts with water to give hydrogen, which can gather under the plate and explode. Keeping the water moving or aerated, and cleaning out aluminium dross as the table maker says, stops it building up.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the spitting arc and short nozzle life?
o: The current is set too low for 3 mm sheet
The work clamp is too close to the cut
Water in the air supply to the torch
The stand-off is set at the maker's figure
questions.why: Water and oil in the air spoil the arc and wear the electrode and nozzle fast. Drain the filter and the compressor tank, fit a dryer if needed, and check the pressure holds when the spray gun runs.

questions.q: What should the helper do when changing nozzles?
o: Keep the machine on, but hold the torch by its handle only
Switch off and isolate the machine first, every time
Wear dry welding gloves and keep the machine running
Switch off at the trigger lock and leave the power on
questions.why: A plasma cutter's open-circuit voltage is much higher than a welding set's, and the parts inside the torch can be live. Consumables are changed only with the power switched off and isolated.

questions.q: What does the heavy, bubbly dross on the aluminium letters show?
o: The travel speed is too slow
The nozzle hole is too small
The air pressure is too high
The travel speed is too fast
questions.why: Low-speed dross is heavy and bubbly and comes off easily. Too fast a speed leaves a small, hard bead rolled under the edge, with sparks spraying up because the cut is not fully through.

questions.q: A welder uses the oxygen hose to blow dust off his overalls before lunch. What should his leading hand tell him?
o: It is fine, as long as the torch is not lit at the time
It is fine outdoors, where the oxygen soon blows away
Use the acetylene hose instead, as it is the safer gas
Stop: clothing soaked with oxygen can burn fiercely
questions.why: Oxygen gets trapped in the cloth, and a spark or cigarette can then set it alight with intense, fast flames. Oxygen is never used as compressed air; a brush or a vacuum cleans clothing.

questions.q: A propane cylinder has a tare weight of 33 kg stamped on it and weighs 46 kg on the scale. How much gas is left?
o: 13 kg
33 kg
46 kg
79 kg
questions.why: LPG is a liquid in the cylinder, so its gauge pressure barely changes until it is nearly empty. Weigh it and take off the tare: 46 − 33 = 13 kg of gas.

questions.q: A farmer brings four jobs. Which one suits oxy-acetylene cutting?
o: A 6 mm aluminium plate for a trailer floor
A 25 mm mild steel plate for a trailer hitch
A cracked cast-iron pump body to cut in two
A 3 mm stainless sheet for a milk tank cover
questions.why: Mild steel burns in the oxygen jet and its oxide melts below the steel. Aluminium and stainless steel form oxides that melt far above the metal, and cast iron melts before it burns, so those jobs need plasma or a saw.
